revised_evidence.revised_excerpt: A neuromechanical simulation couples a neural controller to a mechanical model of the body it controls. Motor-neuron activity recruits actuators, the resulting forces move or load the joints, and sensory pathways carry measurements of that response back to the controller. I wanted to transfer a locomotor circuit from one model of the legs to another. A circuit that alternates the legs in suspension must also coordinate muscle force with foot contact if the model is to support weight. I developed tools to inspect that loop one connection at a time and to repeat a mechanical test after changing a connection.

I built on OpenSim, MyoConverter, MuJoCo, SNS-Toolbox, Simulink, and Simscape \citep{delp_opensim_2007,caggiano_myosuite_2022,todorov_mujoco_2012,nourse_sns_2023}. My contribution was to prepare mechanical models, implement editable neural and actuator blocks, connect neural outputs with actuator commands and mechanical measurements with sensory inputs, and write drivers that repeat interventions with a saved controller. The methods below describe how to assemble an experiment. The results start with a single joint, then examine how sensory return and mechanical assistance change bilateral coordination. Appendix~\ref{app:simulation_verification} gives the executable examples and scoring definitions.

The methods below describe how to assemble an experiment. The results start with a single joint, then examine how sensory return and mechanical assistance change bilateral coordination. Appendix~\ref{app:simulation_verification} gives the executable examples and scoring definitions.

I used two routes to prepare the mechanics. For imported musculoskeletal models, I converted OpenSim geometry and muscle paths with MyoConverter and checked the result in MuJoCo. For CAD assemblies, I used joint frames, inertial properties, and attachments to assemble mechanisms for Simscape Multibody or, separately, MuJoCo. A researcher can also run a Simulink controller against existing MuJoCo mechanics through the runtime bridge. That route exchanges commands and measurements at each update and requires an executable MuJoCo model.

\noindent\begin{minipage}{\linewidth}Table~\ref{tab:sns_capability} gives a starting point for each type of experiment. The graphical tools expose individual connections and their signs. The scripts run the same circuit and intervention repeatedly without a graphical interface. A saved set of parameters and a recording link a result to the controller that produced it.

I implemented the SNS-Simscape library as editable Simulink blocks for neurons, synapses, sensory encoding, activation, and actuator force (Figure~\ref{fig:simulink_sns_implementation}). The graded equations follow SNS-Toolbox \citep{nourse_sns_2023}. Each synapse sends a conductance and its product with reversal potential to the postsynaptic neuron. This makes the sign and strength of a connection available for inspection. From the \path{Code/Matlab/SNS_Simscape/gui} directory, running \verb|app = SNSGui()| opens my circuit editor. A user can place and connect graded neurons, save the circuit description, and generate a Simulink circuit through \path{sns_build_from_json.m}. Separate builders connect complete reflex circuits to the knee and arm dynamics.

The graphical editor's Build action imports the saved graded neurons, synapses, and external current destinations into Simulink. A user can inspect each connection's conductance, reversal potential, and activation ramp. The separate demonstration builders add mechanical equations, actuator blocks, and sensory wiring. The worked knee experiment below uses the coupled model generated by its demonstration builder.

The MathWorks MuJoCo--Simulink C++ S-function exchanges command and measurement arrays with an existing MuJoCo mechanism. independent_findings.rationale: Original zero of twelve averaged-channel checks, later 48 individual channel-cycle checks at nominal cadence, six adaptive replay cadences, and failed or guarded coupled trials have distinct protocols. The chronology explains why a fitted downstream output could hide a PF failure.

revised_evidence.revised_excerpt: {\interlinepenalty=10000 In the human-model controllers s3k and syn6, the fitted motor output concealed a PF timing error. In the original syn6 evaluation, none of twelve channels passed the combined timing criteria. Three components per side explained \qty{99}{\percent} of the centered variance in transmitted PF activity, compared with six components for the intended primitives. One channel remained active throughout the cycle. The corresponding s3k signals required two components per side, but that design lacked quantitative target windows against which to score individual channels.\par}

{\interlinepenalty=10000 Adjusting synaptic gains alone improved the syn6 fit without bringing any of its twelve channels within the timing criteria. RG-triggered relays and native SNS timing circuits addressed the timing directly. At nominal cadence the native circuit passed all 48 channel-cycle checks. Adaptive timing passed at six prescribed replay cadences. These checks scored individual cycles, including onset and offset, whereas the original twelve checks scored channel means. When live sensory input replaced prescribed replay, coupled trials reached the predictive knee limit or finished without meeting the rhythm and PF timing criteria. The next design question is how sensory input shifts the onset and termination of PF transmission. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_pf_timing} gives the replay and coupled-body tests.\par}

Feedforward and feedback fits in the s3k and syn6 families tested motor output. To test the intermediate PF computation, I measured outgoing transmission, $\operatorname{clip}(V/\qty{5}{\milli\volt},0,1)$, where $V$ is rest-relative membrane voltage. I averaged nine cycles on the original \qty{1.233}{\second} calibration clock, from \qty{2.466}{\second} through \qty{13.556835}{\second}, without shifting individual channels. Transmission above 0.2 defined a burst. Each channel had to match the target burst count, have absolute fundamental lag of at most \ang{30} and duty error of at most 0.15, and span at least 0.2 transmission. These thresholds define the engineering timing test.

None of the twelve syn6 channels met all four requirements. Three components per side captured \qty{99}{\percent} of the centered variance in the measured outputs, compared with six for the target primitives. The fifth primitive stayed active throughout the cycle on both sides despite target duties of approximately 0.325 and 0.330. Two components per side captured the corresponding s3k variance. Its intended onset and duration windows had not been specified, precluding the same target comparison. Figure~\ref{fig:app_pf_timing} shows the timing defects that a downstream activation fit can conceal. The component counts describe waveform variance.

A gain-only repair improved the mirrored-target objective in a fresh process but still passed zero of twelve channels. I kept this candidate out of the body adapter and changed the timing design. RG-event-triggered relays first reproduced the target windows in offline replay. The native SNS version used onset, shutoff, quieting, follower, and ramp cells. Its adaptive version adjusted clock rates from recurring bilateral RG events, combining graded neural computation with an explicit timing scheduler.

The later timing gate scores each of the last four complete ipsilateral RG-E intervals separately, at 200 phase samples per interval. Six channels on two sides give 48 channel-cycle checks. RG-E intervals begin at a \qty{3.5}{\milli\volt} crossing after arming below \qty{1.5}{\milli\volt}. In addition to the original lag, duty, burst-count, and excursion requirements, each onset and offset must lie within 0.05 cycles of its target. This differs from the original twelve checks on cycle-averaged channels. Table~\ref{tab:app_pf_progression} separates the resulting levels of verification. Cadence stress tests scale the legacy-cell integration and RG inactivation constants with the afferent replay cadence, while retaining native relay settings and MN synapses; they do not demonstrate spontaneous cadence adaptation by a freely moving model.

Fixed native timing & 48/48 checks at the nominal \qty{1.233}{\second} cadence; 16/48 at \qty{1.048}{\second} and 8/48 at \qty{1.418}{\second}. \\
Adaptive native timing & 48/48 at each of six replay cadences spanning \qtyrange{0.863}{1.418}{\second}; frozen MN input synapses retained. \\
Adaptive live-body transfer & Predictive knee guard at \qty{9.814}{\second}; 11/30 timing checks after full native handover. \\

Separate physical diagnostics & The same candidate completes \qty{8}{\second} standing and \qty{16}{\second} supported-ground tests; both assessments reject it. \\

After full native handover, three complete right and two complete left RG intervals gave 30 channel-cycle checks. The added knee relay recruits S3 and inhibits S2 near the projected extension limit with the MN input synapses fixed. The saved arrays matched the corresponding fresh native replay and live repeats. Further single-burst S3 candidates still reached the knee guard. No candidate in this series met the PF timing, rhythmic-motion, and knee-safety requirements together in the body.

revised_evidence.revised_excerpt: {\interlinepenalty=10000 The W2L108 robot model, with 108 neurons and 216 connections, took eight qualifying left and seven qualifying right swings on a moving treadmill in \qty{10}{\second}. The qualifying transitions alternated, and each swing unloaded and cleared the whole foot. Minimum anatomical knee flexion over $1\leq t<10$\,s was \ang{2.087} on the right and \ang{1.946} on the left. Upward rail and guide assistance averaged \qty{29.519}{\percent} of body weight in that window. Over the complete trial, signed net assistance averaged \qty{35.069}{\percent}. An independent replay reproduced the selected trajectory. Rails, guides, and belt motion were part of the tested task.\par}

{\interlinepenalty=10000 On the separately assembled CAD robot, an SNS supplied timing while an engineering controller allocated posture, loading, and clearance targets among 54 ideal reference-tension actuators (Figure~\ref{fig:ah001_supported_control}). Over $16\leq t<28$\,s, the model produced seven qualifying right and six qualifying left swings with measured vertical assistance of \qty{77.5}{\percent} of body weight. Lateral and attitude guidance remained active. Minimum knee flexion across the complete \qty{28}{\second} trial was \ang{11.20} on the right and \ang{5.10} on the left. These results test contact handover with prescribed tensile actuation. The separate BPA interface evaluates force from length and pressure.\par}

The human drive-weaning experiment separated a particular descending input from the mechanical assistance. The human model continued to step in place under its support rig when supplementary left and right drive reached zero. The shared descending input remained active. In a separate W2L robot experiment the model progressed with reduced supplementary drive while the harness remained engaged (Appendix~\ref{sec:sns_controller_comparison}).

Suspension removes ground loading. Rails and guides permit contact but carry part of the weight and constrain motion. The evidence for the BiW2Lvar+ air stages, the W2L pathway removal, W2L108 treadmill stepping, and the CAD model's contact handover therefore applies to four distinct experimental conditions. No experiment in this program established harness-free walking.

Morrow and I first transferred the Deng controller to the Li walker in AnimatLab. The legs cycled while suspended and the model tipped when released. The result motivated a practical change in how I tested controllers. I built tools to follow one signal from sensory input through the neural circuit to actuator force and joint motion. In the knee example an extensor Ia pulse produces a measurable extension and recovery. In the supported W2L model, removing the specified sensory inputs and conductances displaced footfalls from antiphase while the body continued to move forward. Recording both contact and movement made the coordination deficit observable.

The human-model drive experiment tested a different dependence. The human model continued to step in place under its support rig with the supplementary left and right hand-drive channels set to zero and the shared descending drive still active. A separate W2L robot model progressed with reduced supplementary drive under its harness (Section~\ref{sec:sns_controller_comparison}). These tests identify which command was removed and what mechanical support the remaining controller had to work against.

In earlier BPA balance-platform experiments, orientation feedback provided a hardware precedent for estimating body attitude \citep{hilts_dynamic_2019,bolen_balance_2024,bolen_selfbalancing_2024,bolen_selfbalancing_srs_2024}. For the biped I would first test whether an estimate of trunk orientation and angular velocity improves recovery from a repeatable disturbance at fixed harness assistance. Adding a visual reference in a second condition would test the effect of correcting inertial drift under the same disturbance. The expected contribution of each signal depends on the task \citep{akay_relative_2021}. Figure~\ref{fig:sensorium_hierarchy} places these proposed pathways above the implemented spinal network.

I calibrated the 108-cell, 216-connection Li--Deng-derived W2L controller for its twelve-muscle walker. In the selected \qty{10}{\second} treadmill trial, eight left and seven right unloaded swings cleared the whole foot, and the qualified transitions alternated. All 32 saved numerical arrays agreed in an independent repeat. Over $1\leq t<10$\,s, minimum anatomical knee flexion was \ang{2.087} right and \ang{1.946} left. These angles incorporate the walker's initial-pose offsets and report flexion as positive.

The passive rails remained in place, with \qty{30}{\milli\meter} of slack in the guides. The continuous harness supplied zero force. Adding the positive vertical contributions of the rails and guides gave \qty{29.519}{\percent} of the \qty{411.2254}{\newton} model weight over $1\leq t<10$\,s. Adding their signed vertical forces over the whole trial, $0\leq t<10$\,s, gave \qty{35.069}{\percent}. The different force definitions and windows account for the two reported measures. The walker advanced \qty{0.908}{\meter} relative to the belt. Peak foot force reached 11.727 body weights, leaving the impact response unresolved.

The robot drive-weaning configuration progressed \qty{1.72}{\meter} in \qty{30}{\second}, retained progression at \qty{60}{\percent} of the supplementary drive scale, and passed twelve perturbed repeats. Mechanical support remained in place, and contact duty fell below the strict walking criterion. The human model retained bilateral stepping in place under the support rig after the added left/right hand-drive channels were removed, with \qty{2.0773}{\nano\ampere} still applied through the shared locomotor-drive input. No harness-free walking was established in these experiments.

revised_evidence.revised_excerpt: {\interlinepenalty=10000 In the human-model controllers s3k and syn6, the fitted motor output concealed a PF timing error. In the original syn6 evaluation, none of twelve channels passed the combined timing criteria. Three components per side explained \qty{99}{\percent} of the centered variance in transmitted PF activity, compared with six components for the intended primitives. One channel remained active throughout the cycle. The corresponding s3k signals required two components per side, but that design lacked quantitative target windows against which to score individual channels.\par}

{\interlinepenalty=10000 Adjusting synaptic gains alone improved the syn6 fit without bringing any of its twelve channels within the timing criteria. RG-triggered relays and native SNS timing circuits addressed the timing directly. At nominal cadence the native circuit passed all 48 channel-cycle checks. Adaptive timing passed at six prescribed replay cadences. These checks scored individual cycles, including onset and offset, whereas the original twelve checks scored channel means. When live sensory input replaced prescribed replay, coupled trials reached the predictive knee limit or finished without meeting the rhythm and PF timing criteria. The next design question is how sensory input shifts the onset and termination of PF transmission. Appendix~\ref{sec:app_pf_timing} gives the replay and coupled-body tests.\par}

A muscle-force comparison can identify a mechanical discrepancy before neural parameters are adjusted. The knee and cup experiments then show what changes when sensory current reaches a motor pool in a model whose load and actuator law are known. By the time a foot touches the treadmill, the same comparison requires a record of contact, actuator force, and external assistance. The progression from one joint to a supported biped makes it possible to ask which part of the loop accounts for a change in behavior.

The W2L sensory intervention illustrates the value of separate outcome measures. The model moved forward under both conditions, although contact timing fell outside the accepted range after the combined removal. In syn6, the opposite problem arose during fitting. An acceptable pattern of motor recruitment concealed a PF channel that remained active throughout the cycle. Recording the signal at the receiving layer distinguished a successful output fit from a circuit that performed its intended function.

The human drive-weaning experiment separated a particular descending input from the mechanical assistance. The human model continued to step in place under its support rig when supplementary left and right drive reached zero. The shared descending input remained active. In a separate W2L robot experiment the model progressed with reduced supplementary drive while the harness remained engaged (Appendix~\ref{sec:sns_controller_comparison}).

The force law also determines what a controller test can establish. The simplified knee actuator isolates the response to a sensory pulse. The BPA20 arm model tests whether the feedback circuit can recruit enough pressure-dependent force as a load increases. Specifying ideal tensions on the CAD model isolates the demands of contact and swing clearance. Applying its controller to physical BPAs introduces a further question about attainable force at each measured length and pressure.

The syn6 result motivates a specific transfer experiment. Record the same PF channel first under prescribed sensory input and then during closed-loop motion. Compare the timing of transmitted output and the knee state when the two responses diverge. This would distinguish a failure of the neural timing circuit under altered input from a mechanical limit that a well-timed command cannot avoid.

For a muscle with poor matched-pose force agreement, a comparison across prescribed movement velocities could separate effects of tendon compliance and activation history. For the robot model, the corresponding experiment would apply a measured pressure history to a characterized BPA route. Repeating a contact or controller test on the repaired model would then show whether the mechanical change affected coordination.

I developed a way to carry a controller from a circuit diagram to a mechanical test with an identifiable input and output. A colleague can repeat the sensory pulse at the knee, disable a pathway on a supported walker, or compare the timing of a PF signal before and after closing the loop. The task, actuator law, and assistance determine which conclusions each of those experiments supports.

Isometric tests establish torque capacity at zero angular velocity. To determine when that capacity can do work, I would measure knee torque $\tau$ and angular velocity $\omega$ on the same time base and about the same signed axis. Their product $P=\tau\omega$, in watts, is the instantaneous mechanical power delivered by the knee to the external load. Positive power indicates energy delivery and negative power indicates absorption. Its timing and magnitude distinguish a knee that supplies energy during extension from one that resists motion to absorb a landing load. A biomechanist can compare these phases with joint-power profiles, and a robot designer can size the actuator for both propulsion and controlled deceleration. A dynamometer on the test stand could drive flexion and extension at prescribed speeds or impose a resisting torque while the BPA moves the knee. An encoder and a joint-axis torque transducer would supply synchronized velocity and torque. Recording actuator pressure and calibrating fixture inertia, friction, and loading-connection compliance would help distinguish pneumatic delay and load--unload hysteresis from losses in the rig.

SADb lets a researcher start with a proposed sensory connection and inspect the experiment behind it. In the Table view, selecting \emph{Ib disynaptic excitation} under \emph{Pathway} returns linked papers. The record for \citet{mccrea_disynaptic_1995} opens a curation note, its pathway links, and the article DOI. In decerebrate cats, stimulating the plantaris nerve inhibited medial gastrocnemius motoneurons at rest. During the extensor phase of midbrain-evoked fictive locomotion, the same stimulation excited these synergist motoneurons. In an acute spinal preparation treated with clonidine, inhibition decreased without the short-latency excitation. The record also links to \emph{Ib disynaptic inhibition}. Reading the original experiment shows why those two links belong together and why a controller designer would test a state-dependent group~I pathway. The stimulation recruited group~I afferents and did not isolate Ib input.

The monthly literature watch supplies candidates for manual curation (Section~\ref{sec:sadb_methods}). For a pathway such as extensor group~I excitation, the most useful addition to a record would be a direct link from each reported sign to its preparation, stimulus, and phase. A reader could then distinguish a measured reversal from an assumption in a computational model before following their citation links. The Bubble map already identifies citation communities by color. Grouping their papers spatially would provide a second way to locate related studies \citep{bolen_using_2024}.

A next controller-transfer test would stimulate the same RG, PF, or MN pathway under prescribed sensory replay and during closed-loop motion. A phase shift at the rhythm generator would distinguish a reset from a skipped motor burst with preserved rhythm (Section~\ref{sec:app_layer_stimulus}). Physiological and modeling studies provide reference responses for such experiments \citep{selionov_tonic_2009,rybak_modelling_2006,markin_afferent_2010,shevtsova_modeling_2016}. Repeating the protocol with the same unaffected synaptic gains, mechanical support, and perturbation would locate where the responses diverge.

In earlier BPA balance-platform experiments, orientation feedback provided a hardware precedent for estimating body attitude \citep{hilts_dynamic_2019,bolen_balance_2024,bolen_selfbalancing_2024,bolen_selfbalancing_srs_2024}. For the biped I would first test whether an estimate of trunk orientation and angular velocity improves recovery from a repeatable disturbance at fixed harness assistance. Adding a visual reference in a second condition would test the effect of correcting inertial drift under the same disturbance. The expected contribution of each signal depends on the task \citep{akay_relative_2021}. Figure~\ref{fig:sensorium_hierarchy} places these proposed pathways above the implemented spinal network.

My longer-term goal is a robot that can perform a kickflip. The knee must deliver power during takeoff, the controller must estimate orientation in the air, and the legs must absorb energy when contact resumes. Those are three identifiable experiments on the way from a stationary torque measurement to a coordinated whole-body maneuver.

Details on the biomimetic robot knee used in this study can be found in \citep{steele_biomimetic_2018,steele_development_2017,steele_biomimetic_2018-1}. In brief, this 1-DoF joint (Figure~\ref{fig:ICR}) uses a four-bar linkage to change the effective moment arm during rotation. The intersection point of the internal crossed links define the instantaneous center of rotation (ICR). This causes the joint ICR location in the femur frame to translate posteriorly in the $X$ direction and distally in the $Y$ direction except for a brief proximal move near full flexion. Reference International Society of Biomechanics (ISB) coordinate frames are given by \citet{wu_for_1995,wu_isb_2002}. This is similar to how the human knee behaves \citep{bolen_determination_2019,morrow_optimization_2020,seth_opensim_2018,delp_opensim_2007,delp_interactive_1990}. The correct location of the ICR is important for both theoretical and experimental torque calculations.

This causes the joint ICR location in the femur frame to translate posteriorly in the $X$ direction and distally in the $Y$ direction except for a brief proximal move near full flexion. Reference International Society of Biomechanics (ISB) coordinate frames are given by \citet{wu_for_1995,wu_isb_2002}. This is similar to how the human knee behaves \citep{bolen_determination_2019,morrow_optimization_2020,seth_opensim_2018,delp_opensim_2007,delp_interactive_1990}. The correct location of the ICR is important for both theoretical and experimental torque calculations.
